intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35), also known as tyrosine kinase 2 (TYK2) deficiency, is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the TYK2 gene.

paragraphs.text: Immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35), or TYK2 deficiency, is an autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiency. Its core feature is susceptibility to intracellular bacteria and/or viruses. The bacteria include mycobacteria (bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG) and Mycobacterium tuberculosis), Salmonella, and Brucella. The viruses include herpesviruses. Kreins et al. (2015) attributed these infections to impaired cellular responses to IL-12 and IFN-alpha/beta. The first patient reported had features of hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES), including atopic dermatitis, high serum IgE, and staphylococcal infections (Minegishi et al., 2006). However, most patients reported later did not have HIES (Kilic et al., 2012; Kreins et al., 2015), and Kreins et al. (2015) concluded that HIES does not appear to be an intrinsic feature of TYK2 deficiency.

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) gave further clinical details on the patient of Minegishi et al. (2006) (P1), a Japanese man born to consanguineous parents. He had atopic dermatitis from the age of 1 month and recurrent bacterial and viral infections from the age of 1 year. These included BCGitis at age 22 months (6 months after vaccination), repeated Staphylococcus aureus skin abscesses, pneumonia without pneumatocele formation, otitis, and sinusitis. At age 15 years he was hospitalized with sepsis after severe nontyphi Salmonella enterocolitis. He also had parainfluenza virus-3 pneumonia, recurrent oral HSV infections with tonsillitis, molluscum contagiosum, and mild oral candidiasis. Laboratory studies repeatedly showed hypereosinophilia (701-800/microliter) and high serum IgE (1,430-2,100 IU/ml). He was diagnosed with autosomal recessive HIES based on an NIH score of 48 points. At age 30 years he had ocular sarcoidosis.

paragraphs.text: Kilic et al. (2012) reported a Turkish boy born to healthy first-cousin parents. He was vaccinated with BCG at age 2 months. Left axillary lymphadenopathy appeared at 8 months, and generalized lymphadenopathy and fatigue followed at 21 months. On admission he had fever and enlarged, fistulous lymph nodes in the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions, and M. bovis BCG was isolated from the draining cervical sinuses. His BCG disease responded to antimycobacterial treatment. At age 8 years he developed Brucella meningitis, with blood and CSF cultures positive for Brucella. The sequelae were severe hearing loss, severe cognitive impairment, and lacunar infarcts on MRI. At 11 years he had herpes zoster of the right maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve, which was treated with acyclovir. He had no skeletal or dental features of HIES and no atopy, asthma, candidiasis, boils, folliculitis, or cold abscesses. Serum IgE measured at ages 2, 11, 16, and 18 years was normal or slightly high (80, 115, 218, and 155 IU/ml, respectively). Kilic et al. (2012) noted that, unlike the Japanese patient, their patient had none of the cardinal features of HIES. They suggested that TYK2 deficiency be considered in patients with BCG disease or other intramacrophage infections, particularly with unusually severe herpesvirus infections, even when HIES features are absent.

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) reported 7 additional TYK2-deficient patients (P2-P8) from 5 unrelated families from Turkey, Morocco, Iran, and Argentina. P2 was the Turkish patient reported by Kilic et al. (2012). P3 and P4 were Moroccan sibs born to first-cousin parents. P3, a girl, developed disseminated extrapulmonary tuberculosis at age 13 years. She had ascites and a psoas abscess from which M. tuberculosis was isolated, and she died after bacterial meningitis, 15 months after symptom onset. Her brother, P4, had meningitis of unknown etiology at age 8 months, recurrent otitis and urinary tract infections, asthma, eczema of the ear canal, and high eosinophil levels. P5, a boy born to consanguineous Iranian parents, had right axillary lymphadenitis at 2 months and multiple cervical lymphadenitis at 4 months after BCG vaccination. At 4.5 years he developed paravertebral and psoas abscesses with pulmonary involvement. His younger sister (P6) had BCG lymphadenopathy after vaccination and, at age 1 year, an unidentified viral skin infection. P7, a 9-year-old Iranian girl born to consanguineous parents, had miliary tuberculosis. P8, an 11-year-old boy from Argentina, had herpes gingivostomatitis, recurrent aseptic (herpes) meningitis, and disseminated cutaneous herpetic lesions, as well as mild mental disability of uncertain origin. None of P2 through P8 had documented staphylococcal or other pyogenic infections or fungal infections, including mucocutaneous candidiasis, and serum IgE was never high. Kreins et al. (2015) concluded that the core clinical phenotype of TYK2 deficiency is mycobacterial and/or viral infection.

paragraphs.text: Wu et al. (2020) reported a Chinese boy born to young nonconsanguineous parents. After BCG vaccination on day 3 of life, he had repeated abscess and ulceration at the injection site. At 14 months he was hospitalized with enlarged left axillary lymph nodes, which showed acid-fast bacilli, and M. bovis BCG was isolated from the draining sinuses. From age 6 months he had recurrent respiratory tract infections, with pneumonia or upper respiratory tract infection every 1 to 2 months, and diarrhea. Pathogens identified included Salmonella, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and M. bovis BCG, and IgM antibodies to influenza A and B viruses were positive. He had no high serum IgE (27.4 IU/ml), atopy, staphylococcal disease, or lymphopenia, but CD3-CD16/CD56+ natural killer cells were low. He began to say simple words at 3 years 4 months, his motor development was normal, and he had a small head circumference. Wu et al. (2020) reviewed 12 reported TYK2-deficient patients. Of these, 58% had intracellular bacterial infections and 58% had recurrent viral infections. Markedly increased serum IgE was reported in 3 (25%), and EBV-related B-cell lymphoma and T-cell lymphopenia in 2 (17%). None of the 12 had the facial features, abnormal bone development or pathologic fractures, delayed loss of deciduous teeth, or aneurysms seen in STAT3-related HIES.
